**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

**Surah al-Muzzammil**

Its purpose is to inform that good deeds repel dangers and fears, and lighten heavy burdens, especially standing before the Exalted King and devoting oneself to His service in the darkness of the nights. He is the best God for accepting deeds and words, for erasing the shadows of misguidance, and the greatest helper in patience and endurance against the troubles that come in the abode of passing away, the place of departure and removal. Its name, al-Muzzammil, is the clearest indication of this theme.

**(In the name of Allah)**, the One who suffices whoever puts his trust in Him in all circumstances.
**(The Most Gracious)**, who encompassed all with the blessing of creation and of clear expression, to the guided and the misguided alike, in all circumstances.
**(The Most Merciful)**, who singled out His party with rectitude in words and deeds, so as to bring them to the abode of perfection.

* *

When the previous surah, al-Jinn, mentioned the glorification of the Revelation, and that among its glorification is the preservation of the one to whom it is sent from all the calamities that would prevent him from conveying it, through what He, glory be to Him, possesses of comprehensive knowledge and power, and the appointment of His Prophet, whom He had raised to His message and made aware of what He willed of His unseen, (ﷺ), at the beginning of this surah He called him to take up the burdens of prophethood, through communion with this Revelation at a time of intimacy and seclusion with the beloved, and of expansiveness and radiance for the one who knocks at the door. This is for ascent and return, and it prepares him to bear the burdens of the message and strengthens him against the heavy task of dealing with the people of misguidance. He spoke using the particle suitable for both nearness and distance, which is specific to the fact that only matters of the greatest magnitude follow it, indicating that he (ﷺ) is meant here with the utmost nearness, through matters far removed from ordinary human reach, being extraordinary breaches of customary norms and of familiar regularities. As for *tazammul* (wrapping oneself in a garment), although it is one of the means toward that, it is among ordinary matters, so it falls short of what is intended by the preparation for that readiness. He was addressed by *tazammul* because it is incompatible with standing in prayer:

﴿O you who wrap yourself up﴾, that is, you who have concealed his person and veiled his affair, and what We commanded him, by what the *tazammul* indicates, whose meaning is wrapping oneself in a garment over the whole body, concealment, and remaining in one place. It also implies that he is lying prostrate on the ground, as he (ﷺ) said concerning the slain of [Uhud]: "Wrap them in their garments and their blood." Along with this there is an indication of concealment too, through the assimilation of the *ta'* of the *tafa''ul* form. Perhaps the assimilation also indicates that the covering with the garment did not encompass the whole body, as will come in al-Muddaththir. Moreover, there is in it an indication of the good news of strength to bear the burdens of what is intended by it. From the saying of the Arabs: *zamala al-shay'* means he lifted and carried it; *al-izdimal* means bearing a thing; *zammaltu al-rajul 'ala al-ba'ir* and similar means I loaded him onto the camel; and *min zamalat al-dabbah fi 'adwiha* means the beast became lively in its running. *Al-zamil* is a wild donkey that seems to limp from its vigor. *Rajul izmil* means a strong man. *Al-zamilah* is a camel on which a man relies to carry his food and goods. It is said of a man knowledgeable in a matter: "He is the son of its camel-caravan (*zawmalatiha*)."

Ibn 'Ata' said: O you who are concealed, what you manifest of the traces of special distinction upon him! This is the time for its revelation. [Ikrimah] said: O you who has borne this matter. Al-Suddi said: He meant, O you who sleep. Others said: This was at the beginning of the Revelation of prophethood, and *al-Muddaththir* at the beginning of the Revelation of the message. Then after that he was addressed as "the Prophet" and "the Messenger."

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 2:**

﴿Stand﴾, that is, in Our service by bearing the burdens of Our prophethood, and by girding yourself with diligence in enduring them. Leave off wrapping yourself up, for that contradicts standing.

Since diligence in service indicates the utmost love, and intention is better than action, and man is created weak, and He, glorified is He, is gentle with this community out of honour for its Imam (ﷺ), He, glorified is He, was pleased from us with sincere turning toward action. He made our rewards greater than our deeds, so He made the reviving of a part a reviving of the whole. He therefore used the name of the whole and intended the part, saying: ﴿the night﴾, that is, the night which is the time of seclusion, privacy and concealment. So pray for Us every night of this kind, and stand before Us in intimate converse, with what We have sent down to you of Our speech, for We want to make you manifest and raise your station on land and sea, in secret and in public. In the Shariah, the meaning of "qiyam al-layl" (night prayer) is the prayer, and therefore He did not restrict it. It comprises all kinds of outward and inward acts, and it is their pillar, so mentioning it indicates what is other than it.

Since the body has a share in rest, He said, excepting from the night: ﴿except a little﴾, that is, from every night. This address was given because when revelation came to him (ﷺ) in the Cave of Hira, he returned to his wife Khadija, may Allah be pleased with her, his heart trembling, and said: "Cover me, cover me!" [I have feared for myself.] She, may Allah be pleased with her, asked him about his condition, and when he related his matter to her, he said: "I feared for myself," meaning that this might be the beginnings of poetry or soothsaying (kahana), and all of that comes from the devils, and that what appeared to him with the revelation might not be an angel. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) hated poetry and soothsaying with extreme hatred. She said to him, and she was a truthful minister: "Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. Indeed you join the ties of kinship, bear the burdens of the weak, provide for the guest, and help in the calamities of truth," and similar words that give firmness. The benefit of wrapping oneself is that when a brave, perfect man is overtaken by a matter that is beyond his strength, and his affair is scattered, he returns to himself, restricts his sight and insight to his own sense, and his powers gather to him; then his good natural disposition grows strong against those imaginary accidents, overcomes them, and returns to the sublime natural disposition, and the physical ailment that had afflicted him departs.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Since the mention of the jinn's conversion had attained an end whose goal and purpose were reached, namely to inform of the acceptance of these and the deprivation of those who were more deserving of acceptance and, outwardly, closer to repentance, after the preceding of their threat and severe intimidation, He turned the speech to the command to him (ﷺ) regarding what is incumbent upon him of the duties of worship and what is incumbent upon him in his remembrances by night and by day, opening that with the most beautiful address and the gentlest mode of speech: ﴿O you who wrap yourself﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1]. This was a consolation for him (ﷺ), as has come: ﴿So let not your soul go out in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], to the end, and so that he might be unconcerned with the obstinacy of those who had been preceded by their obstinacy and the abundance of their disputations. He followed that with what bears witness to this purpose and strengthens it, which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So be patient with patience beautiful﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 5]; ﴿And bear patiently what they say, and forsake them with beautiful forsaking﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 10]; ﴿And leave Me with those who deny, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11]. This is exactly what came in His saying: ﴿So let not your soul go out in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], and in His saying: ﴿We know best what they say, and you are not over them a compeller﴾ [Qaf: 45]. Then He said: ﴿Indeed with Us are shackles﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 12], mentioning what He has prepared for them. If you reflect on these verses, you will find them decisive for what we have put forward, and the coherence of what he mentioned will become clear to you. Then the speech returned to gentleness toward him (ﷺ), peace be upon him, and toward his companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and to the bountiful reward He gives them, despite the shortcomings that occur from those who are fit to glorify the true Deity, majestic is His majesty: ﴿He knew that you would not keep count of it, so He turned to you in forgiveness. So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. Then He concluded the surah with seeking forgiveness for all that preceded of the obstinacy of the deniers, whose mention came earlier in the surahs before, to a degree that the believing servants cannot fulfil, as indicated by His saying: ﴿He knew that you would not keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. — End.

When "the night" (al-layl) was a name for the period between sunset and the break of dawn, and its standing in prayer was extremely burdensome, He, glorified is He, relieved [His servant] of the weight of that. He said, clarifying His intent by what the speech set down after the exception, and making a substitute (badal, apposition) of the whole of the excepted and the excepted from it (p-7): ﴿half of it﴾, that is, the night. Thus it is known that what is meant by the "little" excepted is the half. He called it "little" in relation to the whole night and in relation to the half whose enlivening took place, because what is followed by action is more than what has no action in it. It is also possible that "half of it" is a substitute for "the night," so that it is as if it were said: "Stand [in prayer] half the night, except a little, which is a sixth, or reduce from it to a quarter." This phrasing came thus to convey that whoever stood a third of the night, or rather a quarter of it, or more than that, was enlivening the whole night.

When resolves differ according to persons and according to times, He said: ﴿or diminish from it﴾, that is, from this half which you were commanded to stand [in prayer], or from the half excepted, the little on the second aspect, which is the third, ﴿a little﴾. So do not stand [in prayer] even if you enliven a third of the night [on the first aspect] or its quarter [on the second aspect]; you would be enlivening [all of] it [...] in the bounty of God through multiplication.

[p-8] Or add to it": that is, add a little to the half, such as a sixth, so that what he stands for becomes, for example, two-thirds. Under every one of these estimates, the standing [in prayer] coincides with the time after sleep, which is the time Allah blesses with His manifestation [therein]. It is established that He, glory be to Him, descends in a manner that does not resemble His essence in any way, nor is His descent like the descent of others. Rather, it is a metaphor for the opening of the gate of the heaven, which is a metaphor for the time when supplication is answered, when a third of the night remains, and in another narration, when the latter half of the night remains, to the lowest heaven. He says: "Is there anyone asking, that I may give to him? Is there anyone repenting, that I may accept his repentance? Is there anyone who [needs such-and-such], is there anyone [needs such-and-such]?" until dawn breaks.

This standing in prayer was obligatory upon them at the beginning of Islam, with a choice among these three estimates, and they were burdening themselves. The Prophet (ﷺ) would stand until morning for fear of not preserving the obligatory measure, and likewise some of his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and this became so hard on them that their feet swelled. This was before the obligation of the fifth, and then its last part was revealed with lightening after a year: ﴿He knows that you will not be able to keep count of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and the verses that follow. Thus the standing of the night became a voluntary act after an obligation.

When he was commanded to stand [in prayer] and its time and specific form were determined, he was commanded regarding the manner of recitation, in a general way for the day, informing him that standing in prayer, whose spirit is the Qur'an, [must be done thus]. So He said: ﴿And recite the Qur'an in measured tones﴾, that is, read it deliberately and distinctly between its letters, such that the listener is able to count them, until what is recited resembles a well-arranged set of teeth, which is one with clear gaps, likened to the light of the chamomile. For that is what makes one reflect upon it, so that its essential matters are unveiled for him and its secrets and hidden meanings become clear to him. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Do not scatter it like the scattering of dates, nor rush through it like the rushing of poetry. Rather, stop at its wonders and move hearts with it, and let none of you have his concern be the end of the surah." al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) stood until morning with one verse, and the verse was: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]."

When He, glory be to Him, informed [him] of measured recitation, He informed [him] of its nobility by emphasizing it with the verbal noun, so He said: ﴿measured recitation﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 5:

Since the purpose of this [night prayer] for him ﷺ is the steadfastness of prophethood, and for his community steadfastness in following him in action, in commanding and in forbidding, and since that is extremely difficult, and since a person is powerless except with the help of his Lord, and since beneficial help comes only to one whose soul is purified of turbidities and illuminated with lights, and since that happens only through striving in the service of Him, glorified is He, He gave the reason for this command with His words, explaining the Qur'an which He commanded to be recited, what it is and how it is described, making known that the tahajjud (night prayer) prepares for the soul from the powers that by it one treats hardships, and emphasizing (that what comes is) that which is outside all forms of speech, which can hardly be believed: ﴿Indeed We﴾, that is, with the greatness that is Ours, ﴿shall send down﴾, that is, soon, by a promise that admits no breach, so prepare yourself for that with what is fitting for it.

Since the context calls for an explanation of the difficulty, He expressed it with the particle of elevation, saying: (p-10) ﴿upon you﴾. And along with that He indicated ease, alluding to His words, "And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?" by expressing it with a word whose root revolves around ease and lightness, saying: ﴿a word﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿heavy﴾, that is, because of the arduous obligations in it, from [the aspect of] bearing it and making others bear it, since they oppose natural disposition and contradict the self; and from the aspect of the solidity of its wording, being filled with meanings, together with the sublimity of its meaning and its ascent into obscurity, so that the contemplator does not understand it and extract the jewels within it except with increased thought, purification of the inner secret and stripping of the gaze. So it is heavy upon the one who agrees with it in all these respects and others, and upon the one who opposes it in that he cannot refute it and cannot find any way to criticize it, although it is heavy in the balance, and upon receiving it there is weight, worth and great value. It is narrated in the Sahih: "When revelation came to the Prophet ﷺ, he would be seized by it, and his forehead would sweat profusely on a severely cold winter day. And when revelation came to him while he was riding his she-camel, she would lay down her neck and would hardly move until it had passed from him." Al-Qushayri said: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "Surah al-An'am was revealed to him all at once while he was riding, and his she-camel knelt down from the weight of the Qur'an and its awe." And it, along with its heaviness upon the limbs, is light upon the tongue, easy to recite and to memorize for a human being.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 6:

When this made clear that the tahajjud (night prayer) is of the utmost greatness, he emphasized that, urging against being content with anything less than the best, most beautiful and most perfect, by his saying, emphasizing it so that the matter of standing (in prayer) would be made light upon the self: ﴿Indeed, the rising of the night﴾, that is, its hours, each of which is a nashi'ah (a time of rising), and worship arises in it with the utmost lightness. "Man nasha'" means he rose from his bed with the utmost vigor, owing to the strength of resolve and the keenness of determination, which made it as though it had risen up by itself. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Whatever is after 'Isha' is nashi'ah, and whatever is before it is not nashi'ah." 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "An-nashi'ah is standing (in prayer) after sleep." Al-Azhari said: "An-nashi'ah is standing (in prayer); it is a verbal noun (masdar) following the pattern fa'ilah, like al-'afiyah, meaning al-'afw (pardon)."

Since that was of the utmost difficulty, due to its strong incompatibility with the natural disposition, He increased the emphasis by encouraging it, so He said: ﴿It is﴾, that is, specifically, because of the excellences it possesses, ﴿more firmly rooted﴾, that is, heavier, stronger, sturdier and more solid, ﴿in treading﴾, that is, in hardship and toil, because of what it entails of abandoning comfort and parting from the familiar and the beloved, and firmer in footing. This is on the basis that it is a verbal noun of wat'a, in the reading of the majority, with a fatha then a sukun (waṭ'an); and "muwata'ah" (concord) between the heart and the tongue in presence and in adherence to the religion with submission and humility, on the basis that it is a verbal noun of wati'a (wāṭa'a), like qātil, in the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir, with a kasra and a long vowel (wiṭā'an). [And] it is more eloquent, because the pattern of mufa'alah occurs between two parties who contend with one another, so the action becomes stronger.

Since tahajjud combines speech and action, and since the action is more arduous, and since it is more fitting to precede encouragement with praise, He followed it with speech, saying: ﴿and more upright in speech﴾, that is, more correct in terms of the utterance in its understanding and its impact upon the hearts, through the presence of the heart, the serenity of the night with the quietness of voices, the manifestation of the Lord, glory be to Him and exalted, through the attainment of blessings, and more sincere, free from showing off and base aims.

When He, glory be to Him, had explained from the beginning of the surah up to this point what brings about the righteousness of the religion, which the command [and -] protects, and by which the righteousness of both abodes is achieved, and had shown the virtues of tahajjud (voluntary night prayer), the intended meaning was necessarily: so persevere in it in order to attain these fruits. He said, [giving the reason -], confirming it and explaining what brings about the righteousness of this world, in which one's livelihood lies, and whose righteousness is a means to the righteousness of the intended goal, which is the religion, and which is what befits him, so that he does not become a burden on people, and so that he obtains from provision what helps him in his religion and by which he widens his provision for the dependents of God without weariness, boredom, sluggishness, or excess. He emphasized this because of what the soul has of reluctance towards it: ﴿Indeed, for you﴾, i.e., O one who performs the night prayer, or O most noble of servants if the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, so that it is more emphatic in binding the community to it, ﴿in the daytime﴾, which is the place of striving for the interests of this world.

Since a person exerts himself in his striving for himself with such concern that, because of the intensity of his resolve and the speed of his movement, he is like a swimmer in a medium with no obstacle to him, He said: ﴿a long swimming﴾, i.e., a prolonged turning about over a long span of time. Al-Baghawi said: the root of sabh is swift going. Al-Razi said: ease of movement.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 8:

Since the implied sense is: "so exert yourself in the night prayer (tahajjud)," he follows it with His words, urging the presence of mind (hudur al-fikr): ﴿And mention the name of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to you, who brings you into existence and manages your affairs, by every act that counts as remembrance: by name, attribute, praise, humility, glorification, extolling, prayer, recitation, supplication, devotion to sacred knowledge (ʿilm shar'i), refined good conduct (adab marʿi), and perseverance in all of that. When you magnify the Name through remembrance, you have magnified the One named through tawhid (affirmation of His oneness) and sincerity (ikhlas), and that is a help for you in the welfare of both abodes. As for the Hereafter, it is clear. As for this world, the Prophet ﷺ guided the most beloved of creatures to him, his daughter Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with her), when she asked him for a servant to spare her the hardship, toward glorification (tasbih), praise (tahmid), and magnification (takbir) at the time of sleep.

Since remembrance may occur while one is still attached to others, he informed us that the true rememberer is the one who is absorbed in Him, glory be to Him, and that through this comes complete help. So He said: ﴿And devote yourself﴾, that is, strive to cut yourself off from every preoccupation and to be sincere in all of its deeds, gradually, little by little, ending at: ﴿to Him﴾. Do not cease to be upon that until it becomes a settled disposition (khalq) for you, so that your self is as if cut off without any cutter, and cut off in many ways by every cutter. The sense, guided by the verbal noun "tabattulan" and by His saying "tabtilan," is: he informed by emphasis with the verbal noun, which points to combining the form tafa''ul and the form tafʿil, in intensity of concern and difficulty of the station. It derives from al-batl, which is cutting; a "batlah" charity is one cut off from its owner. For this reason Zayd ibn Aslam said: "Tabattul is renouncing the world and what is in it, and seeking what is with Allah, exalted is He." Maryam, peace be upon her, is called "al-Batul" because she was cut off toward Allah, exalted is He, from all of His creation; likewise Fatimah al-Zahra, also called al-Batul, because she was cut off from any equal, peer, or counterpart. So the meaning here is the same as the meaning of the word of tawhid, which requires turning toward Him and turning away from everything other than Him, by constancy in remembrance and casting off desire. The verse is of ihtibak, which is clear: the mention of the verb "tabattul" is an indication of the omission of its verbal noun, and the mention of the verbal noun of "batala" is an indication of the omission of its verb.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 9:

Since it is obligatory for every person to give thanks to the Bestower of blessings, He (glory be to Him) made clear that He is the One who bestowed the stillness of the night, in which He commanded the tahajjud (night prayer), [and - ] the spreading out of the day, in which He commanded the glorifying of Him (al-sabh). So He said, describing the Lord who is to be remembered, in the recitation of Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and the Kufans other than Hafs, with an emphatic (mu'azzaman lahu) reading in the genitive through the form of a separate sentence (bi-l-qat'), while in the recitation of the rest it is in the nominative (bi-l-raf'): ﴿The Lord of the East﴾, that is, the One who brings into being the place of the lights by which this night in which you stand in prayer is dispelled, and by which the morning is illuminated. "And at dawn the people praise the night journey." By what He has bestowed upon them of lights in the mirrors of their hearts, and by what He has adorned them with meteors of meanings, just as He brought into being for them, on the horizons of their celestial spheres, suns of fruitful meanings, so that companionship may circulate in the abodes of holiness. Thus no star rises in the place that belongs to its Lord except by His permission, and He is the Lord of every place. How excellent is what the Divine Imam Taqi al-Din ibn Daqiq al-Id said:

*How many a night with you we have journeyed through,*
*we know neither closing of the eyes nor rest,*

*and the companions differed over what it is*
*that relieves their complaint or refreshes them,*

*so it was said that their halting for an hour,*
*and I said, rather, your remembrance, and this is the sound view.*

When He mentioned the risings of the lights, because they are the goal due to their clear manifestation, and He used the singular because it better suits the aim of the surah, which is the point where the meaning implied by "wrapped in garments" (al-tazammul) is gathered, He followed it with its opposite, saying: ﴿and the setting﴾, that is, the one from which the night comes, and which is the place of repose, the site of solitude and the sweetness of intimate conversation. So no sun, moon or star sets except by His decree, glory be to Him. And if He is the Lord of that in which these creations exist, which are the most wondrous of creations, then He is the Lord of what is less than that.

When He made known through this that He alone is specialized in governing the existing beings and uniquely in bringing the things that exist into being, He became worthy of being singled out for worship and for turning in complete devotion, so He said, beginning a new statement: ﴿there is no god﴾, that is, no one truly worthy of worship, ﴿but He﴾, that is, your Lord, whose nurturing of you points to the sum of greatness and to the highest attributes of perfection and transcendence above every trace of deficiency. Since He made known His unique oneness, glory be to Him, what befits His servants is that none of them should direct any part of their desire to other than Him. Therefore He made the following consequence of this: ﴿So take Him﴾, that is, take Him with all your effort, by singling Him out, the Exalted, as ﴿a Guardian (wakil)﴾, that is, over everyone who opposes you, by entrusting all your affairs to Him, for He will suffice you in all of them and watch over them to the utmost, since He alone has the power over them, and nothing at all is in the hand of anyone else. So do not be concerned with anything at all. This does not mean that a person should abandon every action, for that is empty desire. Rather, it means a general seeking of whatever the person has been recommended to seek, so that he trusts (mutawakkil) in the means and not apart from means. For otherwise he would be like one who seeks a child without a wife, and this contradicts the wisdom of this world, which is founded upon causes. Even if there were nothing in singling Him out as Guardian except that He differs from human guardians in greatness, nobility and gentleness in every respect, still it would be enough. For your human agent is below you, and you expect him to speak with you often about your interests, while your Lord is the greatest of the great, and He commands you to speak with Him often about your interests and to ask Him at length. Your human agent, when he has gained your wealth, asks you for a wage, while He, glory be to Him, multiplies your wealth and gives you the reward. Your human agent spends on you from your own wealth, while He, glory be to Him, provides for you and spends on you from His own wealth. Whoever holds fast to this verse lives free and noble, dies pure and honoured, and meets God, the Exalted, as a servant who is pure, chosen and devout. It is a condition of the one who affirms God's oneness (muwahhid) that he turn toward the One, devote himself to the One, offer himself to Him in servitude, entrust himself to Him, commit his affairs to Him, leave off managing them himself, trust in Him, lean upon Him, humble himself before His lordship, submit humbly to His greatness, adorn himself with His splendour, and take Him as a refuge ('udda) for every calamity of this world and the next.

(p-18) Since wakalah (entrusting one's affairs to another) applies only to what one cannot manage on one's own, and since the command to adopt it signals that this heavy word (of the Qur'an) must be accompanied by long afflictions, earthquakes and terrors, He said: ﴿And be patient﴾. He pointed to the greatness of patience by linking it with the preposition of elevation, saying ﴿over what﴾, and He lightened the matter by indicating that they can reach no harm beyond verbal abuse; and He magnified it by their persistence in it, saying ﴿they say﴾, i.e., the opponents who are understood from the wakalah, through their repelling of the truth with falsehood regarding the right of Allah and the right of you.

Since keeping away from the hated is permitted only in cases of necessity, it lightens their harm, so He said: ﴿And forsake them﴾, i.e., turn away from them openly, repelling the uproar as much as possible, ﴿with a gracious forsaking﴾, by associating with them outwardly while being separate from them in your inner self and heart, so that you do not mix with them except in what Allah has commanded you, according to the limits He has set for you in calling them to Him, the Exalted, and in attending their joys and sorrows, thereby fulfilling their rights while not demanding your rights from them, neither explicitly nor by allusion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 11:

When his affair involved, through what he does, something very hard, given the possibility that they would be exalted over him, He informed him of the nearness of his relief by threatening them with a swift seizure. So He said: ﴿Leave Me﴾, that is, leave Me to deal with them in whatever state befalls Me in dealing with them. He placed the explicit noun in the position of the pronoun, to attach the ruling to the attribute and to generalize it, and said: ﴿and the deniers﴾, that is, the two groups in denial. For I am capable of both showing them mercy and punishing them.

When He had mentioned their attribute, for which they deserved punishment, He mentioned what drove them to it, to make them unappealing and to turn him away from associating with their people, lest the association become a trial, leading him to take on that attribute and drawing him toward love of this world. So He said: ﴿those of luxury﴾, that is, those who indulge in the comfort of life's ease and pleasure that plenty (al-ni‘ma, with a kasra, meaning bounty and what one enjoys of wealth, children, and status) has bestowed upon them, and the (al-nu‘ma, with a damma, meaning gladness that calls for thankfulness) that they have obtained. They were the greatest of Quraysh and their wealthy.

When the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful, says such a thing about one of His friends, He hastens to destroy his enemy. He said, confirming the purpose of what He commanded him regarding patience with these people in worldly blessings, by stating that their time is short: ﴿and give them respite﴾, that is, leave them gently, patiently, and gradually, and do not concern yourself with their affair.

When He gladdened him with the severity of their threat in this expression, the meaning of which is that He would seize them by His hand, (ﷺ), while He, glory be to Him, is asking Him to delay them, He increased the good news by His saying: ﴿a little﴾, that is, of time and respite, until their death or until they are struck before it. There was a short interval between the revelation of this verse and the Battle of Badr, as al-Muhibb al-Tabari said. In this there is good news for him (ﷺ) that he will remain after their seizure as he was, and that he does not need anything in their affair except that He, glory be to Him and exalted, takes care of them, removing them from his mind, and emptying his outward and inward self for what he is commanded by Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, namely turning wholly toward Allah, glory be to Him. So in the verse there is that whoever occupies himself with his enemy, Allah leaves him to himself, and that this was like an obstacle to Allah's seizing of him. When he places his trust in Him, he has removed that obstacle.

Since this [warning] announces their punishment, and since describing them as possessors of blessing implies that they were accustomed to good foods, and since depriving one accustomed to delicious food does not reach the point of harming the soul as harshly as harming the body unless it is preceded by humiliation, He resumed His speech as an explanation of the kind of punishment that the threat conveyed in general terms. He emphasized it, on account of their denial, with ﴿Indeed﴾, and He indicated the intensity of its strangeness, its majesty, its greatness and its particularity, and its presence was confirmed by His words ﴿with Us﴾ rather than "near Us." And since the hardest thing for a person is to be prevented from what he wishes of freely moving about with his limbs, He said, mentioning what is opposite to the blessing and honor they were in: ﴿shackles﴾, the plural of nikl (with a kasra), which is the heavy fetter that is never removed, as humiliation for them and not out of fear of their escape, as a recompense for their restraining themselves [their souls] through their desires from following the caller, and for their spreading themselves out in walking through the open spaces of their passions. And since that [condition] burns the inner self, He followed it with the burning of the outer self, saying: ﴿and a blazing fire﴾, that is, a fire extremely hot and intensely kindled, on account of what they used to restrain themselves [with] of cooling their drinks, indulging in fine clothing and garments, and laboring at various kinds of comfort.

When he had completed what corresponds to their denial, he followed it with what corresponds to the blessing, saying: ﴿And food that chokes⌋ — that is, one possessing a catching in the throat, like the ḍarī' (a thorny plant) and the zaqqūm (a bitter tree of Hell), which lodges in it so that it does not go down smoothly: it neither descends nor exits, with what they used to strive for in refining foods and drinks and exerting every effort to attain all their aims. And since he specified, he generalized, saying: ﴿and a painful punishment﴾ — that is, [painful —] of intense pain, that leaves them no sweetness in anything at all, in return for what they used to describe their times as, and what they used to trouble those who call them to what benefits them: deliverance from the fetters of sensory perceptions, and ascent from the lowland of desires to the summit of the lasting righteous deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 14:

When He had mentioned this punishment, He mentioned its time, saying: ﴿On the Day when the earth and the mountains quake﴾, meaning they tremble and shake with a violent quaking, ﴿the earth﴾, meaning all of it, ﴿and the mountains﴾, which are the strongest of it. Since the implied sense is: "then the earth will become a level plain, in which you will see no crookedness or elevation," He followed it with His saying: ﴿and the mountains will become a heap of sand﴾, meaning those which are the anchors and pegs of the earth. He expressed the intensity of the mixing and dissolution by the singular, saying: ﴿a heap of sand﴾, meaning gathered sand, a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, from kathabahu (to gather it), when he gathered it. The root k-th-b and k-b-th both revolve around gathering together with nearness, and entail scarcity, for the reality of nearness is the smallness of distance in time or place, and softness. From kathabtu al-turab (I crushed the dust), meaning I rubbed it; and kathaba 'alayhi (in the sense of he carried or charged), meaning he came close to mixing with it; and kathib al-raml (a sand dune), a piece which is pulled along and humped, looking at the smallness in the sense of "a piece." And everything poured out in this way too, because pouring out is customarily for what is small. As for na'am kithab, with the thā' placed first and also placed last, meaning many, it came to him the abundance from the form. The kātibah of a horse is the narrowest place in its width. The kuthbah of the earth is the hollow between mountains, because it is generally small. The kabath, like saḥāb, is the ripe fruit of the arak tree; and it was said: what has not ripened; and it was said: its bearing when scattered. If the ripe is meant, its naming with it is because it is gathered; if what has not ripened is meant, it is from nearness to ripeness; and if the scattered is meant, it is because some of it is near to some, since the arak itself is a small tree. Kabatha al-lahm (kabatha, like fariḥa): it spent the night troubled and so changed, or it became stale, meaning he gathered upon its vessel another vessel, or gathered what was in it until it became cramped, so it is from gathering in this sense. As for al-kunbuth, like qunfudh, with the thā' placed last: the hard, firm one, which is mostly from the gathering of its parts and the interpenetration of some of them into others. Takbith al-safinah is that the ship lean toward the land; it is from gathering and nearness together. As for kathabtu kinānatahu, in the sense of nakathahā (I scattered its arrows), this is a verb used here for removal, meaning he removed their gathering; or in the sense that he brought them close to his throw by arranging them for quick reach.

Since the kathib may sometimes be used figuratively for what is raised, even if it is not soft, He said: ﴿flowing sand﴾, meaning loose, soft, scattered sand, from hālahu (when he scattered it). Al-Kalbi said: it is that which, when you take some of it, what is behind it follows you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 15:

When he had mentioned the punishment and its time, and placed them first so that the listener would attend to what is demanded of him, he followed them with the cause of it, pointing to that by which the affair of the Hereafter is set right, the Hereafter in which is the return, the final end, and the resort. So he said, emphasizing it because of their denial: ﴿Indeed, We have sent to you﴾, meaning with what We have of greatness, ﴿to you﴾, O people of Makkah, as an honour to you in particular, and to everyone the call has reached in general, ﴿a messenger﴾ [i.e.-] (p-٢٤) indeed [and -] he is Muhammad (ﷺ), the seal of the prophets and their leader (ﷺ), ﴿a witness over you﴾, meaning over what you do, so that he may give testimony when it is sought from him, with what is the truth, on the Day ﴿We bring forth from every nation a witness﴾, and that is the Day of Resurrection.

Since this surah is among the earliest to be revealed, when the religion was weak and its adherents were in the utmost of scarcity and humiliation, so that whoever's affair leads him to a time when the religion has become strange, as it was strange at that time, may take a lesson from them. Pharaoh was the most arrogant of people in his time, the most tyrannical, and the most deceitful and cunning. The Children of Israel were in the utmost of subjugation to him and obedience to his command. Yet when God sent to him Musa, peace be upon him, whom Pharaoh had sought to kill by slaying the sons of the Children of Israel, in the hope that he would be among those slain, for it had been said to Pharaoh that a boy would be born among the Children of Israel through whom the destruction of the Qibt (the Copts, the Egyptians) would come, God made him prevail over him, destroyed him despite his strength, and saved the Children of Israel despite their weakness. [God, exalted is He, said] as an admonition to Quraysh, the Arabs, and others, that whoever God is with should not contend, even if he is the weakest of creation, and as an admonition to them to take heed from the state of this tyrant who surpassed them in kingdom, the multitude of armies, and wealth: ﴿As We sent﴾, meaning with what We have of (p-٢٥) greatness, ﴿to Pharaoh﴾, meaning the king of Egypt, ﴿a messenger﴾. Perhaps He made it indefinite to point out that he was not of Pharaoh's people, so nothing prevented him from Pharaoh, neither a close kinsman nor an obeyed intercessor, so that it might be known that whoever has a tribe that defends him is more deserving of help.

When sending the messenger was the cause of either acceptance or rejection, He said: ﴿So Pharaoh disobeyed the Messenger﴾, meaning, because of the crookedness of his nature, ﴿the Messenger﴾, that is, the one of whom We had already said that We sent him to Pharaoh. He had thus become known to you after Moses showed him the clear miracles and the decisive signs. This is what the expression "the manifestation of majesty" (mazhar al-'azamah, the explicit mention of the Majestic Name instead of a pronoun) points to. For this reason, He made His seizing of Pharaoh a consequence of Pharaoh's disobedience, saying: ﴿So We seized him﴾, meaning, by Our majesty. He clarified that the seizing was a taking, a subduing, and a wrath, by His saying: ﴿a heavy seizing﴾, that is, a grievous, severe, oppressive, distressing seizing with a bad outcome. This is taken from the people's saying "wabil" (heavy, injurious) of food, when it is unwholesome and cannot be digested, that is, it does not go down into the gullet (al-mari', the esophagus) and does not sit well in it. This came about by Our destroying him and those with him, all of them, leaving none of them. The rule on the repetition of the indefinite and the definite will come, God willing, in the commentary on "Alam Nashrah".

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 17:

When He knew this, that He (subhanahu) is severe in seizing (punishment), and that the one who strives earnestly will not be benefited by his striving before Him, He (subhanahu) made the following statement a consequence of that, warning them against imitating Pharaoh: (p-26) ﴿Then how will you protect yourselves?﴾ That is, how will you bring into existence the protection that would guard your souls? And since causing aversion through the cause of threat (al-tahdid) is more important, because it is more indicative of the mercy of the one who warns and more effective in prompting avoidance of it, He said, using the particle of doubt to indicate that their disbelief in Allah, despite the rational proofs He has set up for them, supported by transmitted proofs, should not occur in any way, and that it is mentioned only by way of supposition and assumption: ﴿if you disbelieve﴾. That is, if you place a veil over what has been planted in your natural dispositions (fitar) of the lights of the proofs leading to faith, and so you remain upon your disbelief. Moreover, the expression indicates that He has pardoned them for their past disbelief, so He does not reckon it against them, as a mercy and generosity from Him, and only what they committed after the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ) is counted against them. ﴿A Day﴾ [that is,] it is a metaphor for severity, such that it is said of it ﴿that makes the children grey-haired﴾ on account of the intensity of its terrors, its tremors and its frights. ﴿the children﴾, that is, at the time of birth or close to it. ﴿grey-haired﴾ is the plural of ashyab, from ibyaddha sha'ruhu (his hair turned white). This is a metaphor (kinayah) for the abundance of worries in it, because the custom is that when they intensify they hasten whiteness of hair. The meaning is a denial that they could bring about for themselves a protection, by the utmost of their effort, that would shield them from the punishment of that Day, described with this supreme terror, and that is when Allah says: "O Adam, arise and send forth the contingent of the Fire: from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine." And He attributed the making to the Day because the punishment that befalls in it is what is being guarded against, since the Day itself is the setting in which it occurs, just as the one who is wary (al-muttaqi) makes it so.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 73, verse 18:

(p-27) Since this is a momentous matter, he depicted some of its terrors to increase its magnitude, and so said: ﴿The sky﴾, meaning: despite its greatness, its loftiness and the firmness of its construction. Since the intended meaning is the genus that encompasses all of it, he used the masculine and said: ﴿splitting asunder﴾, meaning: cleaving and coming apart from the awe of the Lord, like the separating of beads from a string that has been broken. Had he used the feminine, it would have referred to one of the heavens only. There is also another subtle point in choosing the masculine: it conveys the extra intensity of the terror that leads to its splitting, that it reaches the utmost degree of intensity, because the masculine in everything is stronger than the feminine. All of this is to make the mentioned Day appear terrifying. ﴿Therein﴾, meaning: by the severity of that Day; the bāʾ here indicates instrumentality. It is also permissible for it to mean "in it", meaning that the splitting and cleaving occur in it, through the clouds, the descent of the angels, and other things, including falling and breaking apart under the severity of its firmness. So what then do you think of other than it?

Since this is great, he resumed explaining its insignificance in relation to His greatness, glorified and exalted be He, and so said: ﴿His promise﴾, meaning: the promise of God that was mentioned earlier among the manifestations of His greatness, so the construct is a verbal noun in the sense of its agent. ﴿Is ever fulfilled﴾, meaning: easy and already accomplished, whatever it may be. How much more so when it concerns this Day, which is the locus of wisdom. (p-28) Or the pronoun refers to the Day, and then the construct is in the sense of its object, indicating that the promise that occurs in it and through it is unavoidable, and it is known that it can only be from God.

Since what preceded in this surah of rulings, encouragement and warning has guided toward the noblest character and rescued from every evil, He said, resuming and emphasizing, to alert to its greatness and that it deserves to be drawn attention to: ﴿Indeed, this﴾, that is, the aforementioned portion of this surah, ﴿is a reminder﴾, that is, a great reminder, worthy that the one who takes heed be admonished by it and the one who reflects be instructed by it, and especially what it mentioned of the people of disbelief and the kinds of punishment. Since He, glorified is He, has given man an intellect by which he perceives the good and the bad, and a will by which he is able to follow what he wills, there remains no obstacle for him in choosing what is most beneficial and best except the compulsion of the Will, of which he has no knowledge and over which he has no recourse. Upon this He causes to follow His saying: ﴿So whoever wills﴾, that is, to take heed and be admonished, ﴿takes﴾, that is, takes with the utmost of his effort, ﴿to his Lord﴾, that is, specifically, not to other than Him, ﴿a way﴾, that is, a path that leads him to His portions, because it is free of confusion, so that he travels according to what the reminder has brought him. That holding fast while journeying is by the Book and the Sunnah in accordance with what the Ummah has agreed upon, and whoever deviates from that is ruined.

(p-29) Since some people may go to excess in worship and burden themselves, and at other times may burden others, Allah, glorified and exalted be He, pointed to moderation, to lighten the fatigue that befalls a person. He pointed to what the soul does while it is joined to the body, which is the state of life, because its benefit is to provision itself with every good before the terror of the graves, for the soul is extremely subtle while the body is extremely dense. The soul belongs to the world of command (ʿĀlam al-Amr), in which existence occurs at a single stroke without gradation or development, whereas the body belongs to the world of creation (ʿĀlam al-Khalq). So the soul is a stranger in the body and needs to be made at home, and it is made at home by whatever brings it closer to the spiritual world, free of the attachments of bodies. This is achieved by turning the whole heart away from these lowly things and occupying oneself with remembrance (dhikr), prayers, and all righteous deeds, for that is what helps it join its lofty, precious, and noble world. The greatest help toward this is wisdom (al-ḥikma), which is justice in deeds and moderation in words and actions. So Allah, glorified be He, said, beginning a new statement as an answer concerning the facilitation of the path and its being built on the lenient upright monotheism (al-ḥanīfiyya al-samḥa), such that nothing prevents it except the hand of power: ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾, that is, the one who manages your affairs in what constitutes kindness to you and gentleness toward you and your community, ﴿knows that you stand﴾, that is, in prayer, as you were commanded at the beginning of the surah.

Since abundance of deeds is praiseworthy and scarcity is the opposite, He used a metaphor for the lesser amount, saying ﴿adnā﴾, that is, a lesser period of time. The word adnā is shared between "nearer" and "lower in rank," because each of them entails a smaller distance. ﴿Less than two-thirds of the night﴾ on some nights, ﴿and half of it, and a third of it﴾ [that is:] and less than each of them on some nights. This is according to the reading of the majority (al-jamāʿa). The meaning according to the reading of Ibn Kathir and the Kufans, with the accusative (naṣb), is the specification of the half and the third that fall under "less than two-thirds." On both readings it corresponds to what was left optional at the beginning of the surah, between standing for half of the night in full, or for less than it, which is a third, or for more than it, which is two-thirds, or for a lesser portion of the half, which is a quarter.

When Allah, glorified be He, mentioned His Messenger's standing (ﷺ), He followed it with the standing of his followers. He said, conjoining it to the pronoun hidden in ﴿taqūmu﴾, and the intervening word made it acceptable: ﴿and a group﴾, that is, a group likewise stands, having the capacity for gathering (around you) through their turning toward you and toward one another. Since it is customary that the word "companion" (ṣāḥib) is sometimes applied to whoever is with a person, while not necessarily in the heart, He turned to saying ﴿those who are with you﴾, that is, in their words and deeds, that is, upon Islam. It seems that He chose this rather than saying "among the Muslims," because it is understood that a group did not perform this standing, so He did not wish to call them Muslims. The sense of "being with" (maʿiyya) is more general.

Since standing in this manner, with this variation and with striving to excel in worship, indicates a lack of knowledge of the exact measures of the night, He, exalted be He, said: ﴿And Allah﴾, that is, you stand thus because you do not know the measures of the hours precisely, while the King who encompasses everything in power and knowledge alone ﴿measures﴾, that is, a tremendous measuring that is in the utmost precision, ﴿the night and the day﴾, so He knows every minute of them as they are, because He created them, and nothing of them exists except by Him. ﴿Does not He who created know?﴾ [al-Mulk: 14].

Since He knew from this the hardship upon them in standing at night in this manner, in knowledge and in action, He explained that by saying: ﴿He knew﴾, that is, Allah, glorified be He, ﴿that you would not be able to keep count of it﴾, that is, you would not be able to measure it in knowledge and in action. From this is His Messenger's (ﷺ) saying: "Be steadfast, and you will not be able to keep count." ﴿So He turned to you﴾, that is, as a consequence of this knowledge, He, glorified be He, withdrew by abrogation (naskh, the replacement or lifting of a previous ruling) what He had made obligatory ﴿upon you﴾, by granting you license to abandon the standing measured at the beginning of the surah. That is, He lifted the responsibility from you for abandoning standing according to that measure which He had set, just as He lifts (sin) from the one who repents. He called it "turning" (tawba) though there was no sin, indicating that by its heaviness it is likely to lead to sin.

When He lifted it, He made the command to them dependent upon what would be easy for them, so He said, expressing prayer by recitation because it is its greatest pillar, indicating that the night prayer (tahajjud) is recommended and not obligatory: ﴿So recite﴾, that is, in prayer or otherwise, by night or by day, ﴿what is easy﴾, that is, what is simple and effortless for you, and what is pliant and submissive to you, ﴿of the Qur'an﴾, that is, the Book that gathers everything that benefits you. Al-Qushayri said: It is said, "from five verses onward," and it is said, "from ten verses onward." Al-Baghawi said: Qays ibn Abi Hazim said: "I prayed behind Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in Basra, and he recited in the first rak'a the Fatiha and the first verse of al-Baqara, then he stood in the second and recited the Fatiha and the second verse." It is also said that He commanded recitation alone, establishing it in place of what had been obligatory for them of prayer, with an added ease. Accordingly, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzayma, and Ibn Hibban in his Ṣaḥīḥ narrated from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever stands in prayer with ten verses is not recorded among the heedless; whoever stands with one hundred verses is recorded among the devout (qānitīn); whoever stands with one thousand verses is recorded among the wealthy in reward (muqantarīn)." Al-Mundhiri said: From Surat al-Mulk to the end of the Qur'an is one thousand verses.

Since this was an abrogation of what had been obligatory of the night standing at the beginning of the surah, because of His knowledge that they would not be able to keep count, He explained that general knowledge with detailed knowledge, clarifying another wisdom for the abrogation. So He said: ﴿He knew that﴾, that is, that ﴿there will be among you the sick﴾, meaning by a decree that you cannot avoid. The plural of ḍarīḍ (sick) is marḍā. This surah was among the first revealed to him (ﷺ), so in it is good news that the people of Islam will greatly increase.

When He mentioned the excuse of the sick and began with it, because it is more general and the sick person has no power to ward it off, He followed it with travel for trade, because it comes next in generality. So He said, giving the good news, along with the multiplication of the people of Islam, of the spaciousness of the earth for them: ﴿And others﴾, that is, not the sick, ﴿travel﴾, that is, they strike (the earth) with their feet, ﴿upon the earth﴾, that is, they journey, because one who walks with diligence and effort strikes the earth with his foot. Then He resumed explaining the cause of the travel by saying: ﴿seeking﴾, that is, seeking intensely, and He indicated the vastness of what is with Allah by making it above their hopes, so He said: ﴿of the bounty of Allah﴾, that is, some of what the Supreme King has brought into being for His servants, while He has no need of it in any way, through profit in trade or through acquiring knowledge. ﴿And others﴾, that is, among you, O Muslims, ﴿fight﴾, that is, seek and inflict the killing of the enemies of Allah. Therefore He specified it by saying:
(p-34) ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, that is, that killing is contained within the road of the Supreme King, so that it may remove the obstruction from its path by killing highwaymen, both the spiritual and the physical. He made it explicit rather than implicit, to exalt jihad and so that one would not be confused about returning to trade. This is an exhortation from Allah to us toward mercy for the servants and consideration of their excuses; whoever does not show mercy is not shown mercy. Al-Baghawi said: Ibrahim narrated from Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "Whichever man brings something from one of the cities of the Muslims, patiently and seeking reward, and sells it at the price of its day, he is in Allah's sight in the rank of the martyrs." Then ʿAbdullah recited: ﴿And others travel in the earth seeking﴾, the verse. And from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Allah has created no death that I would die after being killed in the way of Allah more beloved to me than dying between the two halves of a leg while striking the earth, seeking of the bounty of Allah."

Since these were other excuses that call for license, or causes for not keeping count, He ordered upon them the previous ruling, so He said, emphasizing the recitation and explaining its greater magnitude: ﴿So recite﴾, that is, each one of you ﴿what is easy﴾, that is, for you ﴿of it﴾, that is, of the Qur'an. He omitted it (the noun) to inform that it is the very same as what came before, so the obligation became standing for a part of the night in the manner of facilitation. Then that was abrogated by the five daily prayers. Since it was suitable that by it could be meant the prayer, because it is the greatest of its pillars, and that by it could be meant the recitation itself without an additional prayer as a further facilitation, He said, favoring the second interpretation (p-35) or explicitly indicating the first: ﴿And establish﴾, that is, bring about the establishment of ﴿the prayer﴾, the obligatory one, with all matters by which it stands: its pillars, its conditions, its preliminaries, its completions, its forms, its embellishments, and its perfecting elements.

When He reminded (them) of the attribute of the Creator, which is one of the two pillars of Islam, the physical and the financial, He followed it with the other pillar, which is the link among creatures, so He said: ﴿And give﴾ from the good of your wealth which We have bestowed upon you ﴿the zakāt﴾, that is, the obligatory one. Since the intended meaning is the known obligatory zakāt, He followed it with all the obligatory and recommended expenditures, so He said: ﴿And lend to Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King who possesses all attributes of perfection, among which is absolute richness, from your bodies and your wealth in times of your health and affluence, ﴿a goodly loan﴾ from the voluntary good deeds in their entirety throughout His law, with complete willingness, and in a beautiful manner in its beginning, its end, and all its circumstances. For it is preserved for you with Him, blessed in it, so that He may return it to you multiplied at the time you most need it.

Since this religion is comprehensive, and this Qur'an is wise because its Revealer possesses the attributes of perfection, He commanded in these phrases the principal deeds, showing concern for them. (p-36) He followed that with a general command encompassing all the laws of the religion, so He said: ﴿And whatever you put forward﴾, and He urged sincerity of intention by saying: ﴿for yourselves﴾, that is, specifically, in advance, for the sake of what comes after death, which you cannot do (except by the deeds) ﴿of good﴾, that is, whatever good it is, of acts of worship of the body and of wealth, ﴿you will find it﴾ preserved for you ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the One who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿it is﴾, that is, not other than it, ﴿better﴾, that is, for you. The occurrence of "khayr" (better) as a separated element between two non-definite forms is permitted, because "afʿal min" (comparative form) is like a definite noun, and for that reason the definite article is prohibited from being attached to it.

Since everyone who does good is rewarded for it, whether at the time of death or in life, whether a disbeliever or a Muslim who is sincere or not, if he is sincere his reward is in the Hereafter, and otherwise it is in this world, He said: ﴿and greater in reward﴾, that is, than what is given to one who makes a bequest during the illness of death, and [it is] such that one is recompensed for it in this world.

Since a person, when he does what is praised, especially when the one praising him is his Lord, may be seized by self-admiration (ʿujb), He explained to him that he cannot in any way measure Allah with the true measure, so he will always be deficient, and nothing is sufficient for him except pardon, indeed forgiveness. So He said, urging that the conclusion of deeds be seeking forgiveness and acknowledging shortcoming in serving the Proud, the Compeller, indicating the state of the soul's separation from the body, and that its well-being is rest from every evil: ﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah﴾, that is, ask for and bring about the covering of the Supreme King, whom you cannot encompass in knowledge of Him, ﴿how much less﴾ the fulfilling of the due of His service, because of your shortcoming both in essence and in effect, in doing what pleases Him and avoiding what angers Him.

When he understood from the context and from the expression "the Greatest Name" (al-ism al-a'zam, the Most Great Name of God) that He, glory be to Him, is so exalted in His majesty that the one who asks Him might despair of being answered, he gave the reason for the matter in His words, emphasizing it to bring closer what the one who calls to mind His majesty, glory be to Him, and the severity of His retribution and the strength of His seizing would find unlikely: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾. He made explicit, to inform that His attributes are not limited in their effects to those who seek forgiveness, nor to every asker in general, ﴿is All-Forgiving﴾, meaning He is absolute in covering the very sins and their effects, so that no reproach or punishment remains upon them, ﴿Most Merciful﴾, meaning He is absolute in honoring after covering, through bounty, goodness, dignity and grace.

This surah has included an explanation of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning what he was given of comprehensive speech: "[O Allah,] set right for me my religion, which is the safeguard of my affair; set right for me my worldly life, in which is my livelihood; set right for me my hereafter, to which is my return; make life an increase for me in every good, and make death a rest for me from every evil." Each of its clauses has been indicated in its place. The surah has also ended, with the encouragement to act and the mention of its reward, by returning to its beginning: the command to stand before Him, and the allusion of seeking forgiveness, to the greatness of the station, even if the deed is great and lasting, and even if it is performed by standing in the darkness of the nights while people are asleep. So glory be to Him, to whom belongs this speech that is inimitable for all of mankind, because of His encompassing of majesty and generosity. Glory be to Him, the God who mends hearts that are broken.
